### The Zee Admission and the Field-Wide Scope of the Blind Spot


The Stay–Baez 2010 thread is not an isolated case. The same structural gap is acknowledged — explicitly, in print — in one of the most widely-read graduate quantum-field-theory textbooks of the past two decades: Anthony Zee's *Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell* [Zee2003]. Zee writes, in the section on imaginary time and finite-temperature field theory:

> *"Surely you would hit it big with mystical types if you were to tell them that temperature is equivalent to cyclic imaginary time. At the arithmetic level this connection comes merely from the fact that the central objects in quantum physics $e^{-iHT}$ and in thermal physics $e^{-\beta H}$ are formally related by analytic continuation. Some physicists, myself included, feel that there may be something profound here that we have not quite understood."*

This is a foundational admission in a canonical textbook from one of the senior figures of theoretical physics. Zee — Princeton-trained, decades of contributions to gauge theory, condensed matter, and gravity — states explicitly that the connection between temperature and imaginary time is "formally related by analytic continuation" with "something profound here that we have not quite understood." The admission is structurally identical in content to what Stay and Baez were asking in 2010: the Wick rotation $iT \leftrightarrow \beta$ is a formal substitution whose physical meaning is not understood. Zee published this in 2003 and the second edition in 2010 [Zee2010]; the admission has stood unrevised through the editions of one of the field's most cited textbooks.

The community-physics tradition exhibits the same gap. The August 2021 Reddit thread "Is there a physical interpretation of a Wick rotation?" on the *r/AskPhysics* community forum [AskPhysics2021] asked the same question and received the canonical orthodox answer in its top-voted reply: *"Nah, there's no physical interpretation. It's made possible only by the technical Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction theorem, and the fact that the path integral in Minkowski space is not 100\% well-defined while the Euclidean one is. Then the correspondence between Euclidean QFT and statistical mechanical models is exact (at least near critical points), and the Boltzmann factor $\leftrightarrow \hbar$ correspondence becomes exact."*

This reply is the standard orthodox position: the Wick rotation has no physical interpretation; it is a technical tool justified by a reconstruction theorem [OsterwalderSchrader1973, OsterwalderSchrader1975]. The reply is structurally a *$dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel retreat* of the same kind as the Johnson-Freyd 2010 reinterpretation of Stay's question as Feynman-diagram asymptotics: it gives a formal mathematical answer (the path integral in Minkowski space is poorly defined; the Euclidean one is; the reconstruction theorem allows passage between them) without addressing the physical question (what is the imaginary time, structurally?). The Osterwalder–Schrader theorem is an Algebraic Channel theorem — it operates on operator-algebraic / functional-integral machinery (reflection positivity, OS axioms) and produces an Algebraic Channel correspondence (Euclidean QFT $\leftrightarrow$ Hilbert-space QFT). It does not — and cannot — supply the physical content of the imaginary time, because the Algebraic Channel is constitutively time-symmetric.

The Reddit thread accordingly exhibits the same blind spot as the 2010 *n-Category Café* thread and as Zee's textbook admission. ### The Pre-Wick Genealogy of $t \to -i\tau$: From Poincaré 1905 Through Schrödinger 1931 to Wick 1954


The previous subsection identifies Poincaré 1905/1906 and Minkowski 1908 as the historical moments at which the $+ic$ perpendicularity content of $dx_4/dt = ic$ first appeared in canonical literature, with Poincaré supplying the mathematical structure and Minkowski supplying the geometric and ontological interpretation, and Wick 1954 as the moment at which the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ was formalized as a calculational tool in relativistic bound-state physics. The standard contemporary narrative — exemplified by the 2026 Wikipedia article [Wikipedia2026WickRotation] and circulating widely in physics pedagogy — telescopes this history, attributing the "first implicit use" of the Wick rotation to Schwinger and Feynman in the late 1940s. The narrative is historically wrong by approximately forty-four years. The Wick rotation as a coordinate substitution was first used by Henri Poincaré in 1905, three years before Minkowski; it was used as an explicit connector between quantum wave evolution and Markovian diffusion by Erwin Schrödinger in 1931, eighteen years before any Schwinger or Feynman use; and it was formalized in finite-temperature field theory by Takeo Matsubara in 1955, one year *after* Wick. The correction of the historical record is structurally important because the genealogy of $t \to -i\tau$ traces a chain of near-misses spanning fifty years between 1905 and 1955, every one of which is a $dx_4/dt = ic$ Geometric Channel observation made without the active-expansion content of $dx_4/dt = ic$. We trace the chain in order, with primary sources.

**Poincaré 1905 — the first introduction of $ict$ as a fourth coordinate.** Henri Poincaré's June 5, 1905 *Comptes Rendus* note "Sur la dynamique de l'électron" [Poincare1905CR], expanded into the bulky December 1905 / 1906 *Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo* memoir of the same title [Poincare1906Rendiconti], is the historically first introduction of $ict$ as the fourth coordinate of a relativistic four-dimensional space. Poincaré observed that the Lorentz transformations leave the quadratic form $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2t^2$ invariant, and explicitly noted that they could be regarded as rotations in a four-dimensional space with coordinates $(x, y, z, ict)$. Damour's modern historical reading [Damour2017] confirms the priority: Poincaré's 1905 note presents the four-dimensional formalism three years before Minkowski's 1908 Cologne address. The June 1905 publication date predates Einstein's June 30, 1905 *Annalen der Physik* paper "Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper" by approximately three weeks. Poincaré's 1905/1906 formulation is therefore the historical origin of the imaginary-time substitution $t \to ict/c = it$ that the contemporary Wick-rotation literature attributes to the late 1940s. The substitution Poincaré used in 1905 is identically the substitution the orthodox literature calls the Wick rotation; the only difference is that Poincaré used it as a relativistic-electrodynamics coordinate identification, not as a calculational device for analytic continuation of quantum amplitudes.

**Minkowski 1908 — the geometric and ontological interpretation, not the four-dimensional formalism itself.** Minkowski's September 21, 1908 Cologne address "Raum und Zeit" [Minkowski1908], published in 1909 in *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, is conventionally credited with the introduction of four-dimensional spacetime. The conventional credit is inaccurate at the level of primary sources. The four-dimensional formalism with imaginary fourth coordinate $ict$, the Lorentz transformations as rotations in that four-dimensional space, the invariant quadratic form $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2 t^2$, the Poincaré group of transformations (formally treated as a group, before Minkowski), the first four-vectors (including a four-current and a four-force), and even the first analysis of gravitation propagating at $c$ with corresponding gravitational waves — all are present already in Poincaré's 1905/1906 *Comptes Rendus* note and *Rendiconti* memoir [Poincare1905CR, Poincare1906Rendiconti], three years before Minkowski's Cologne lecture. The modern historical analysis by Damour [Damour2008Minkowski] and the comprehensive primary-source study by Walter [Walter1999NonEuclidean] establish that Minkowski's mathematical formalism contains essentially no new content beyond Poincaré's 1905/1906 results at the level of the four-dimensional coordinate-and-transformation machinery itself.

What Minkowski added is a layer of geometric and ontological interpretation built on top of Poincaré's already-existing mathematical formalism. Six items of genuine addition are identifiable in the primary sources. (1) The phrase and concept of *spacetime* (*Raum-Zeit*) as a single physical entity rather than a mathematical four-dimensional space: the Cologne lecture's famous opening declaration that *"henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality"* is an ontological claim about physical reality, not a mathematical observation. Poincaré had the four-dimensional mathematical structure but explicitly did not believe it carried physical reality; Damour [Damour2008Minkowski] documents that *"although the first discovery of the mathematical structure of the space-time of special relativity is due to Poincaré's great article of July 1905, Poincaré (in contrast to Minkowski) had never believed that this structure could really"* be physically substantive. (2) The *spacetime diagram* — the visual representation with worldlines, light cones, past and future hypercones, simultaneity hyperplanes — is genuinely Minkowski's introduction; Walter [Walter1999NonEuclidean] establishes that Minkowski's Figure 1 from the Cologne lecture is new and that Poincaré had no such diagrams. (3) The concept of the *worldline* (*Weltlinie*) as the fundamental physical object — a particle's history is its worldline, not a sequence of (position, time) pairs — is Minkowski's. (4) *Proper time* $\tau$ as the invariant parameter along a worldline, enabling correct four-velocity and four-acceleration definitions, is Minkowski's. Walter notes that Minkowski's first attempt at four-velocity in his 1907 colloquium was actually wrong; he corrected it for the 1908 *Grundgleichungen* paper using proper time. (5) The *light cone as a global causal structure* — the recognition that the locus $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - c^2 t^2 = 0$ partitions spacetime into causally distinct timelike-past, timelike-future, and spacelike-elsewhere regions — is Minkowski's. (6) The *full four-tensor calculus for electrodynamics*, with the electromagnetic field tensor $F_{\mu\nu}$ and its dual emerging cleanly from the four-dimensional formalism, is developed in Minkowski's April 1908 *Grundgleichungen* paper to a depth Poincaré had not reached.

The six items are interpretively decisive but mathematically modest extensions of Poincaré's 1905/1906 content. Minkowski himself did not cite Poincaré in the Cologne lecture; Damour [Damour2008Minkowski] identifies this omission as a structural failure of the lecture, and Born subsequently reported that Minkowski had told him the 1905 Einstein paper *"came to him as a great shock"* because Minkowski had reached the same conclusions independently but had not published, *"because he wished first to work out the mathematical structure in all its splendour."* Minkowski never made a priority claim against Einstein or Poincaré; the historical record positions Minkowski as the figure who supplied the geometric and ontological interpretation while Poincaré had supplied the mathematical formalism.

The structural reading for the McGucken framework is sharper than the conventional credit allows. The $+ic$ perpendicularity content that the present paper identifies as load-bearing appears in *Poincaré's 1905/1906 formulation*, not in Minkowski's 1908 reading; the mathematical content of $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) as the imaginary fourth coordinate of a Lorentz-invariant four-dimensional space is Poincaré's, three years before Minkowski. Minkowski's six interpretive additions — spacetime as physical entity, worldlines, spacetime diagrams, proper time, light cones, four-tensor electrodynamics — are themselves consequential, and they made the four-dimensional formalism intelligible to the physics community in a way that Poincaré's purely mathematical presentation had not. But the imaginary-time content itself — the substitution $t \to ict/c = it$ that becomes the Wick rotation forty-six years later — is in the historical record from June 5, 1905, three years before Minkowski's Cologne lecture. The McGucken framework's recognition that $x_4 = ict$ is the integrated coordinate shadow of an active physical-geometric process $dx_4/dt = ic$ is therefore an extension of *Poincaré's* 1905/1906 mathematical structure with the active-expansion content that neither Poincaré nor Minkowski possessed. Poincaré had the mathematics and rejected the physical interpretation; Minkowski had the geometric interpretation and rejected the dynamical content; the McGucken framework supplies the dynamical content as the foundational physical principle, recovering both the mathematical structure (Poincaré 1905/1906) and the geometric interpretation (Minkowski 1908) as theorem-shadows of $dx_4/dt = ic$.

**Sommerfeld 1909 — further development.** Arnold Sommerfeld's 1909 work [Sommerfeld1909] further developed Minkowski's four-dimensional formalism, specifically applying the $ict$ method to the addition of velocity vectors in special relativity. Sommerfeld's work made the four-dimensional formalism a working tool of relativistic physics, with $ict$ as the fourth coordinate used routinely throughout the 1910s and 1920s. The Born–Pauli school used $ict$ as standard notation; Pauli's 1921 *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften* article on relativity theory [Pauli1921Encyclopedia] systematically uses $X = (x, y, z, ict)$ as the standard four-position vector. The $ict$ formulation was the dominant convention in special relativity for approximately twenty years, from Poincaré 1905 through Einstein's gradual transition to the real-coordinate $(-,+,+,+)$ metric tensor formulation during the development of general relativity 1913–1916.

**Schrödinger 1931 — the first explicit $t \to -i\tau$ connector between quantum mechanics and diffusion.** Erwin Schrödinger's 1931 paper "Über die Umkehrung der Naturgesetze" [Schrodinger1931], delivered to the Prussian Academy of Sciences and published in the *Sitzungsberichte*, is the earliest extant explicit use of the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ as a connector between quantum wave evolution (Schrödinger's own 1926 wave equation) and Markovian diffusion (the Smoluchowski–Fokker–Planck heat equation). Schrödinger recognized — five years after publishing the wave equation — that his equation with the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ becomes a diffusion equation, structurally identical to the heat equation of statistical physics. The 1931 paper poses what is now called the *Schrödinger bridge problem*: the question of how to construct a stochastic process whose marginal distributions match given initial and final probability distributions, via the analytic continuation of quantum wave evolution. The modern review by Chetrite, Muratore-Ginanneschi, and Schwieger [ChetriteEtAl2021] establishes Schrödinger 1931 as the foundational paper of what is now called the Schrödinger-bridge program in stochastic optimal transport [Leonard2014]. The substitution $t \to -i\tau$ Schrödinger used in 1931 is identically the substitution Wick used in 1954 and is identically the substitution the contemporary literature calls the Wick rotation.

Schrödinger 1931 is the closest pre-McGucken near-miss in the historical record. Schrödinger had the wave equation; he had the diffusion equation; he had the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ that connects them; he had explicitly noted that the two equations are related by this substitution. What he did not have was the recognition that $\tau = x_4/c$ is a coordinate identity on a real four-dimensional manifold whose fourth axis is physically expanding at $+ic$. Schrödinger treated the substitution as a *formal* connector — a mathematical relation between two equations — rather than as a coordinate-geometric identity with physical content. The Cascade of Near-Misses subsection of the present paper (treating Schrödinger 1926–1944 as the founder's two near-misses) is the structural diagnosis of this gap: Schrödinger came closer than any other pre-McGucken figure to the recognition, and his failure to close the gap is the precise diagnostic of why the orthodox formalism has been unable to supply the physical content from inside.

**Kac 1949 — the Feynman–Kac rigorous formulation.** Mark Kac's 1949 paper "On distributions of certain Wiener functionals" [Kac1949] is the rigorous mathematical formulation of what Schrödinger had observed informally in 1931: the matrix elements of the heat-kernel operator $e^{-t\hat H}$ acting on the Schrödinger Hamiltonian $\hat H = -\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V$ admit a path-integral representation in terms of Wiener-process expectations. Kac was directly motivated by Feynman's 1948 paper "Space-time approach to non-relativistic quantum mechanics" [Feynman1948], which had introduced the Lorentzian path integral $\int \mathcal{D}\gamma \exp(iS[\gamma]/\hbar)$. Kac recognized that under the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ Feynman's formal path-integral expression becomes the rigorously-defined Wiener-process expectation $\int \mathcal{D}\omega \exp(-S_E[\omega]/\hbar)$, with the Brownian motion measure of Wiener 1923 [Wiener1923] supplying the rigorous mathematical content that Feynman's formal expression lacked. The Feynman–Kac formula is now standard mathematical physics; its 1949 publication establishes that the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ — fourteen years before Schrödinger 1931 and forty-four years after Poincaré 1905 — was a working tool of mathematical physics in 1949, well before the Schwinger 1958 and Wick 1954 papers that the contemporary narrative attributes the rotation to.

**Wick 1954 — the Bethe-Salpeter formalization.** Gian-Carlo Wick's 1954 *Physical Review* paper "Properties of Bethe-Salpeter Wave Functions" [Wick1954] is the paper that gave the rotation its name. Wick's specific application was *not* the connection between quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics — the application that the contemporary literature most often associates with the Wick rotation. Wick's application was the *relativistic two-body bound-state problem* in quantum electrodynamics: the Bethe-Salpeter equation [BetheSalpeter1951] for hydrogen-like bound states with relativistic kinematics. Wick observed that the integration contour in the energy plane could be rotated by 90 degrees from the real axis to the imaginary axis, converting the Minkowski-signature Bethe-Salpeter equation into a Euclidean-signature integral equation that was tractable by standard techniques. The Wick 1954 paper is therefore a *technical* paper on relativistic bound states, not a *conceptual* paper on the QM–statistical-mechanics correspondence. The name "Wick rotation" attached to the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ across all of its uses retrospectively, by analogy with Wick's energy-contour rotation in the Bethe-Salpeter integral.

The historically accurate statement is therefore: Wick 1954 introduced the *name* and the *Bethe-Salpeter application*; the *substitution* itself had been used continuously since Poincaré 1905, with substantive intermediate applications by Schrödinger 1931 (quantum-to-diffusion) and Kac 1949 (Feynman path integral to Wiener integral). The contemporary literature's attribution of the "first implicit use" to Schwinger and Feynman in the late 1940s is wrong by approximately forty years if Poincaré 1905 is the starting point, and approximately twenty years if Schrödinger 1931 is taken as the starting point.

**Matsubara 1955 and Schwinger 1958 — the finite-temperature formalization.** The application of the rotation specifically to the finite-temperature field theory — the application that the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster identifies as the structural mystery — was developed by Takeo Matsubara in 1955 [Matsubara1955] (the Matsubara-frequency formalism for finite-temperature quantum statistical mechanics) and by Julian Schwinger in 1958 [Schwinger1958] (the "On the Euclidean Structure of Relativistic Field Theory" paper that introduces the Schwinger functions as analytic continuations of Wightman functions). These are the papers in which the operator-correspondence $e^{-i\hat H t/\hbar} \leftrightarrow e^{-\beta \hat H}$ at the heart of the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster first appears in its modern form. Matsubara is one year after Wick; Schwinger is four years after Wick. Both Matsubara and Schwinger built on Wick's contour-rotation observation, applying it to the finite-temperature regime that Wick himself had not addressed.

**Symanzik 1969 and Osterwalder–Schrader 1973/1975 — the rigorous axiomatization.** Kurt Symanzik's 1969 work on Euclidean field theory [Symanzik1969], followed by Konrad Osterwalder and Robert Schrader's 1973 [OsterwalderSchrader1973] and 1975 [OsterwalderSchrader1975] reconstruction theorems, supplied the rigorous mathematical axiomatization of Euclidean quantum field theory and its analytic continuation back to Minkowski space. Osterwalder–Schrader established the reflection-positivity condition under which the analytic continuation is rigorously valid; the reconstruction theorem of Osterwalder–Schrader 1975 establishes that a Euclidean field theory satisfying the OS axioms reconstructs a unique Wightman quantum field theory in Minkowski space. The OS axioms are the modern standard mathematical justification for the Wick rotation as a calculational tool; they are formal-mathematical the $dx_4/dt = ic$ Algebraic Channel content without physical-geometric the Geometric Channel content. The McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ (Theorem 6 of [MGWick]) is the Geometric Channel content that complements the Algebraic Channel OS axiomatization (Theorem 6.1 of [MGUnification], the Signature-Bridging Theorem).

**The genealogy table.** The complete pre-McGucken genealogy of the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ is:

- 1905 — Poincaré introduces $ict$ as fourth coordinate in *"Sur la dynamique de l'électron"* (relativistic electrodynamics) [Poincare1905CR, Poincare1906Rendiconti]
- 1908 — Minkowski extends Poincaré's formal observation to four-dimensional geometric formalism with $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) (special relativity, geometric interpretation) [Minkowski1908]
- 1909 — Sommerfeld further develops the $ict$ method for relativistic velocity-vector addition [Sommerfeld1909]
- 1921 — Pauli's *Encyklopädie* article uses $X = (x, y, z, ict)$ as standard notation [Pauli1921Encyclopedia]
- 1923 — Wiener constructs the rigorous Brownian-motion measure on path space [Wiener1923]
- 1931 — Schrödinger explicitly uses $t \to -i\tau$ to connect quantum wave evolution and Markovian diffusion [Schrodinger1931]
- 1948 — Feynman publishes the Lorentzian path integral $\exp(iS/\hbar)$ [Feynman1948]
- 1949 — Kac formalizes the Feynman–Kac formula connecting Feynman path integrals to Wiener integrals via $t \to -i\tau$ [Kac1949]
- 1953 — Feynman applies Wick-rotated Euclidean techniques to the polaron problem [Feynman1953Polaron]
- 1954 — Wick formalizes the energy-contour rotation in the Bethe-Salpeter equation; the substitution gets his name [Wick1954]
- 1955 — Matsubara introduces the imaginary-time formalism for finite-temperature quantum statistical mechanics [Matsubara1955]
- 1957 — Kubo formula for linear response, beginning of the KMS-condition story [Kubo1957]
- 1958 — Schwinger introduces Euclidean field theory in *"On the Euclidean Structure of Relativistic Field Theory"* [Schwinger1958]
- 1959 — Martin and Schwinger introduce the KMS condition for thermal field theory [MartinSchwinger1959]
- 1965 — Feynman and Hibbs publish *Quantum Mechanics and Path Integrals* with the "amusing result" passage on statistical mechanics from path integrals [FeynmanHibbs1965]
- 1969 — Symanzik develops the rigorous Euclidean field theory program [Symanzik1969]
- 1973 — Osterwalder and Schrader publish the reconstruction axioms for Euclidean Green's functions [OsterwalderSchrader1973]
- 1975 — Osterwalder–Schrader reconstruction theorem completed [OsterwalderSchrader1975]

The genealogy is fifty years long from Poincaré 1905 to Matsubara 1955 (the canonical operator-correspondence application), and seventy years long from Poincaré 1905 to Osterwalder–Schrader 1975 (the canonical rigorous axiomatization). Across this entire span, the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ was a working tool of mathematical and theoretical physics, used in relativistic electrodynamics, geometric special relativity, quantum-mechanical wave evolution, stochastic processes, Feynman path integrals, relativistic bound states, finite-temperature field theory, and rigorous Euclidean quantum field theory. *In no instance during the seventy-year period from 1905 through 1975 was the substitution recognized as a coordinate identity on a real four-dimensional manifold whose fourth axis is physically expanding at velocity $c$.* The recognition is supplied by the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$; without it, the substitution is a formal device with deep calculational utility and no physical content.

**The diagnostic.** The pre-Wick genealogy makes the Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster's persistence even more striking. The substitution that the cluster identifies as the structural mystery has been a working tool of physics since 1905. Across one hundred and twenty years (1905 to 2025), every senior figure who has used the substitution — Poincaré, Minkowski, Sommerfeld, Pauli, Wiener, Schrödinger, Feynman, Kac, Wick, Matsubara, Schwinger, Osterwalder, Schrader, Symanzik, Huang, Zee, Wolfram — has either treated it as a formal device (Poincaré, Wick, Matsubara, Schwinger, Osterwalder, Schrader, Symanzik) or recognized it as carrying unidentified physical content (Schrödinger, Feynman, Huang, Zee, Wolfram). The Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster is the residue of the second group: those who saw the structural significance of the substitution but lacked the physical principle that would make the significance precise. The McGucken Principle is the physical principle; the McGucken-Wick rotation $\tau = x_4/c$ is the precise content; the cluster is closed.

The historical record's standard narrative — that "the Wick rotation was first implicitly used in the late 1940s by Schwinger and Feynman" — is therefore a structural artifact of the same blind spot the cluster diagnoses. The narrative telescopes a century-long genealogy into a half-decade window because the senior figures of the late 1940s (Feynman, Schwinger, Kac) were the first to use the substitution *in the regime where its physical content is most apparent* (quantum field theory and statistical mechanics), and the narrative inherits the orthodox framing that treats Poincaré's and Minkowski's prior use as "merely relativistic notation" with no connection to the QM–statistical-mechanics correspondence. The McGucken framework dissolves the telescoping: the substitution $t \to -i\tau$ is *one substitution*, with *one physical meaning* — the coordinate identity $\tau = x_4/c$ on the real four-manifold $\mathcal{M}$ — across all of its applications from Poincaré 1905 through Osterwalder–Schrader 1975 through the contemporary literature. The Poincaré application (relativistic electrodynamics), the Schrödinger application (quantum-to-diffusion), the Feynman application (path integrals), the Wick application (Bethe-Salpeter bound states), the Matsubara application (finite-temperature field theory), and the Schwinger application (Euclidean field theory) are all instances of the same coordinate identity, with $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) as the real fourth coordinate of a manifold whose fourth axis is physically expanding at velocity $c$. The unification of these applications is the structural content the orthodox formalism has lacked for one hundred and twenty years.


### Einstein's Rejection-Then-Acceptance of Minkowski Spacetime: The Substantivalist Question Einstein Could Not Resolve


A structurally diagnostic episode in the historical record of $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) that the pre-Wick genealogy understates is the precise arc of Einstein's relationship with Minkowski's geometric reading of special relativity between 1908 and 1916. The standard popular narrative — that Einstein first rejected Minkowski's four-dimensional formalism, then later accepted it — is correct at the headline level but compresses and distorts the structural content. The primary-source record establishes a more diagnostic position: Einstein's rejection was not a temporary misjudgment that he later corrected through deeper understanding; it was a sustained philosophical commitment to anti-substantivalism about spacetime that Einstein maintained throughout his life, with the 1912–1916 "acceptance" being a *technical-mathematical* adoption of Minkowski's machinery for the construction of general relativity rather than a *philosophical-ontological* endorsement of Minkowski's reading.

**Einstein 1908: "überflüssige Gelehrsamkeit" — superfluous learnedness.** Einstein's earliest documented reaction to Minkowski's 1908 Cologne address was the dismissal of the four-dimensional geometric formalism as *"überflüssige Gelehrsamkeit"* — superfluous learnedness or superfluous erudition. The quote is attested in Abraham Pais's canonical biography *Subtle is the Lord: The Science and Life of Albert Einstein* (Oxford University Press, 1982, p. 151–152) [Pais1982] and repeated in essentially every reputable history of relativity from Sommerfeld's contemporary recollections forward. Einstein's own 1908 paper with Jakob Laub on the electromagnetic foundations of relativity in moving bodies — "Über die elektromagnetischen Grundgleichungen für bewegte Körper" [EinsteinLaub1908] — contains a structurally diagnostic phrase: *"we do not consider it superfluous to derive here these important equations in an elementary way, which is, by the way, essentially in agreement with that of Minkowski."* The word *superfluous* is doing the load-bearing work; Einstein is conceding the formal agreement with Minkowski while explicitly framing his own elementary algebraic approach as not-superfluous, with the unstated implication that Minkowski's geometric approach is.

**Einstein 1910–1912: "Since the mathematicians have invaded the theory of relativity, I do not understand it myself any more."** Sommerfeld's contemporary recollection adds a second documented Einstein complaint: in conversation around the 1910 period, Einstein remarked that *"Since the mathematicians have invaded the theory of relativity, I do not understand it myself any more"* [Sommerfeld1949Recollections]. The remark, addressed at the Göttingen mathematical formalization program that included Minkowski's geometric reading and Hilbert's subsequent variational reformulation, documents Einstein's sustained position through the 1908–1912 period as one of methodological resistance to the four-dimensional geometric formalism. Einstein's mathematical training at the ETH Zurich (1896–1900) had included Minkowski as a teacher, and Minkowski's well-documented opinion of Einstein at the time was *"Oh, that Einstein, always cutting lectures... I really would not believe him capable of it"* [BornMinkowskiRecollections]. The student-teacher relationship was distant; the intellectual relationship after 1908 was, from Einstein's side, dismissive.

**Einstein 1912: the turning point under mathematical necessity, not philosophical conversion.** The canonical historical scholarship dates Einstein's switch to the four-dimensional formalism to the summer–autumn of 1912 [Weinstein2012Turning, Norton2012Conjecture]. The turning point is documented in Einstein's October 29, 1912 letter to Sommerfeld in which he describes his switch of attitude toward mathematics. By the summer of 1912 Einstein had concluded that general relativity required tensor manifolds, that gravitation could not be described by a variable speed of light (his Prague 1911 attempt) but had to be described by the metric tensor field, and that the natural arena for the metric tensor was precisely Minkowski's spacetime. Marcel Grossmann (Einstein's classmate at the ETH and by then professor of mathematics at the Zurich Polytechnic) supplied the Ricci-Levi-Civita absolute differential calculus that became tensor calculus, and the 1912/1913 Einstein-Grossmann *Entwurf* paper [EinsteinGrossmann1913] is the first joint publication in which Einstein systematically uses the four-dimensional spacetime formalism rather than the algebraic kinematic approach of 1905.

The 1912 turn is therefore not a philosophical conversion to Minkowski's substantivalist reading of spacetime; it is a *technical adoption of Minkowski's mathematical machinery under the necessity of constructing general relativity*. Einstein needed tensor manifolds; Minkowski had supplied a pseudo-Riemannian manifold of spacetime; Einstein adopted the machinery. The Brown–Pooley analysis [BrownPooley2004] develops this point philosophically and at length: Einstein viewed Minkowski spacetime as a calculational arena, not as a substantive physical entity, and continued to do so for the rest of his life.

**Einstein 1916: the canonical credit to Minkowski in the general-relativity review.** Einstein's full acknowledgment of his debt to Minkowski's geometric formulation appears in the 1916 review *"Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie"* [Einstein1916GR] — the canonical statement of general relativity. Einstein credits Minkowski's four-dimensional formulation as essential to the new theory; the credit is genuine and the indebtedness is real. But Einstein's mature philosophical position on spacetime as a physical entity, expressed in his 1922 *The Meaning of Relativity* lectures [Einstein1922Meaning] and his 1924 essay [Einstein1924Aether], maintains a critical line. Einstein writes in 1922 that it is *"contrary to the mode of scientific thinking, to conceive of a thing... which acts itself, but which cannot be acted upon."* Spacetime in special relativity is such a thing — a fixed background that influences matter (through inertial structure) without being influenced by matter — and Einstein viewed this as a structural defect that general relativity partially repairs (by making spacetime dynamical through the metric tensor's coupling to matter) but does not fully resolve. Einstein's 1916 acceptance of Minkowski is *technical-mathematical* and *partial*; the *philosophical-ontological* commitment to Minkowski's substantivalism is what Einstein continued to resist.

**The structural diagnostic: Einstein closer to Poincaré than to Minkowski.** This is the diagnostic point for the McGucken framework. Einstein's actual position throughout his life is consistent with one specific reading: *he accepted Minkowski's geometric machinery as a calculational tool while rejecting its physical-ontological substantiveness.* He never made the move Minkowski's Cologne lecture explicitly demands — that *"space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows, and only a kind of union of the two will preserve an independent reality"* — as a philosophical commitment. For Einstein, spacetime remained a mathematical convenience over which real physics played out, with the four-dimensional formalism justified by its calculational utility rather than by its ontological status. This puts Einstein structurally *closer to Poincaré's position than to Minkowski's*: both Poincaré and Einstein had the mathematics and rejected the deep physical-ontological reading. Poincaré rejected it explicitly (per Damour [Damour2008Minkowski]: *"Poincaré (in contrast to Minkowski) had never believed that this structure could really"* be physically substantive). Einstein rejected it implicitly via the action-reaction critique and through his sustained anti-substantivalist philosophy. Minkowski was the outlier who elevated the geometric structure to physical reality, and he did so without recognizing the dynamical content. Three figures, three positions, none with the active-expansion content of $dx_4/dt = ic$.

**Einstein's exaltation of $x_4 = ict$ in the relativity books: the primary-source canonical passage.** It is structurally important to record that despite Einstein's philosophical resistance to substantivalism, his 1920 *Relativity: The Special and General Theory* [Einstein1920Relativity] (written December 1916, English translation by Robert W.\ Lawson published by Methuen \& Co Ltd, London, 1920; the canonical popular-exposition statement of Einstein's mature 1916/1920 position) and his 1923 *The Meaning of Relativity: Four Lectures Delivered at Princeton University, May 1921* [Einstein1923Princeton] both *exalt Minkowski's $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) throughout the general-relativity exposition*. The primary-source passage from §XVII ("Minkowski's Four-Dimensional Space") of the 1920 book is structurally diagnostic and bears quoting in full:

> *"The discovery of Minkowski, which was of importance for the formal development of the theory of relativity, does not lie [in the four-dimensional reading per se]. It is to be found rather in the fact of his recognition that the four-dimensional space-time continuum of the theory of relativity, in its most essential formal properties, shows a pronounced relationship to the three-dimensional continuum of Euclidean geometrical space. In order to give due prominence to this relationship, however, we must replace the usual time co-ordinate $t$ by an imaginary magnitude $\sqrt{-1}\cdot ct$ proportional to it. Under these conditions, the natural laws satisfying the demands of the (special) theory of relativity assume mathematical forms, in which the time co-ordinate plays exactly the same role as the three space co-ordinates. Formally, these four co-ordinates correspond exactly to the three space co-ordinates in Euclidean geometry. It must be clear even to the non-mathematician that, as a consequence of this purely formal addition to our knowledge, the theory perforce gained clearness in no mean measure."* [Einstein1920Relativity, §XVII]

And the closing passage of the same section:

> *"These inadequate remarks can give the reader only a vague notion of the important idea contributed by Minkowski. Without it the general theory of relativity, of which the fundamental ideas are developed in the following pages, would perhaps have got no farther than its long clothes."* [Einstein1920Relativity, §XVII]

These two passages are Einstein's own canonical exposition explicitly stating that the substitution $t \to \sqrt{-1}\cdot ct$ — equivalently $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) — is the load-bearing formulation under which the time coordinate "plays exactly the same role as the three space co-ordinates," and that Minkowski's work was the structural prerequisite *without which* general relativity *would have got no farther than its long clothes* (i.e., would have remained in infancy). The structural reading is sharp on three counts. *First*, Einstein himself locates the essential content of Minkowski's contribution in the recognition that the four-dimensional spacetime continuum has a "pronounced relationship to the three-dimensional continuum of Euclidean geometrical space" — a relationship that is made manifest *only* by the substitution $x_4 = ict$. *Second*, Einstein writes that under this substitution "the time co-ordinate plays exactly the same role as the three space co-ordinates" — the four-fold equality of the coordinates is exactly the perpendicularity content that the McGucken framework identifies as the structural source of $dx_4/dt = ic$. *Third*, Einstein assesses Minkowski's contribution as load-bearing for general relativity — "without it the general theory of relativity... would perhaps have got no farther than its long clothes" — a metaphor from infant clothing that frames Minkowski's $x_4 = ict$ formulation as the prerequisite for general relativity's maturation rather than as a notational convenience.

The structural significance is sharp: Einstein in 1920 and 1923, while still maintaining philosophical anti-substantivalism about spacetime in his more philosophical writings [Einstein1922Meaning, Einstein1924Aether], *used and exalted Minkowski's imaginary fourth coordinate $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) as the load-bearing formulation* of general relativity in his canonical popular exposition. The contemporary $(-,+,+,+)$ real-signature convention had not yet displaced the $x_4 = ict$ formulation; Einstein's own books from 1920 through the 1923 Princeton lectures present the $ict$ form as primary, with the four-fold equality of the coordinates as the essential formal content.

The McGucken framework's reading of this passage is direct. Einstein's 1920 statement that under $x_4 = ict$ "the time co-ordinate plays exactly the same role as the three space co-ordinates" is the precise formal content of the McGucken Principle's four-fold equality at the level of the integrated coordinate shadow. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ is the dynamical content underlying Einstein's 1920 formal observation: the reason the time coordinate plays exactly the same role as the three space coordinates under $x_4 = ict$ is that $x_4$ *is* a fourth spatial-perpendicular coordinate, dynamically expanding at velocity $c$ from every event. Einstein had the formal observation in canonical print in 1920; he did not have the dynamical content that explains *why* the formal observation holds. The McGucken framework supplies that content.

The historical residue is therefore: Einstein in 1908 dismissed Minkowski's geometric formalism as superfluous learnedness; Einstein in 1912 adopted it under mathematical necessity; Einstein in 1916 credited it canonically in the general-relativity review; Einstein in 1920 and 1923 *exalted* Minkowski's $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) throughout his own books on relativity; and Einstein throughout his life maintained philosophical anti-substantivalism about spacetime. The arc is real but it is not the simple "rejected then accepted" arc of the popular retelling; it is a more structurally interesting position of *technical acceptance combined with philosophical resistance*, with Einstein's actual published exposition of relativity using $x_4 = ict$ as the load-bearing formulation while his philosophical writings continued to deny that the structure should be read as a substantive physical entity.

**The McGucken position.** The McGucken framework supplies what Einstein, Poincaré, and Minkowski all lacked. Poincaré had the mathematics with explicit anti-substantivalism. Einstein had the mathematics with implicit anti-substantivalism. Minkowski had the geometric-ontological substantivalism without the dynamical content. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ recovers Einstein's $x_4 = ict$ from his own 1920/1923 books as the *integrated coordinate shadow* of an active physical-geometric process, where the active expansion is the dynamical content all three figures lacked. The substantivalism Einstein resisted is correct — but with the load-bearing modification that the substance is not a static four-dimensional manifold but a dynamically expanding fourth axis with the spatial three-manifold as its instantaneous Huygens-wavefront cross-section. The McGucken framework therefore does not reject Einstein's philosophical position; it shows that Einstein's anti-substantivalism was directed at the *wrong target*. The target Einstein critiqued — spacetime as a fixed background that acts without being acted upon — is precisely the *static* reading of Minkowski's geometric structure. The McGucken Principle replaces the static reading with a dynamical reading: $x_4$ is not a fixed background; it is actively expanding at $+ic$ from every event. The expansion *is* the action of the manifold; the matter coupled to $x_4$ via the Compton frequency $\omega_C = mc^2/\hbar$ (Theorem 4 of the present paper) *acts back* on the structure by determining its local content. The action-reaction principle Einstein required is restored: the manifold acts on matter through the active expansion; matter acts on the manifold through its Compton-coupled $x_4$-oscillation. Einstein's 1916 critique of Minkowski's static substantivalism is vindicated; Minkowski's substantivalism is rescued by making the substance dynamical; the McGucken Principle is the synthesis Einstein was searching for but did not find.

**The Einstein 1912 *Manuscript on the Special Theory of Relativity*: the canonical primary source for $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$) in Einstein's own hand.** Beyond the 1920 *Relativity* book examined above, there exists an earlier, more diagnostic primary-source document: Einstein's 1912 *Manuscript on the Special Theory of Relativity*, the unpublished holographic manuscript Einstein composed in 1912 as a textbook-style exposition of special relativity, lost for decades and rediscovered in the late twentieth century, published in facsimile and English translation by George Braziller in 2004 [Einstein1912Manuscript]. The 1912 manuscript carries unique evidentiary weight in the present argument because, unlike the 1920 popular exposition (written in the wake of general relativity's completion), the 1912 manuscript is contemporaneous with Einstein's turning point — composed in the same year as the October 29, 1912 letter to Sommerfeld documenting Einstein's switch of attitude toward mathematics [Weinstein2012Turning]. The 1912 manuscript is therefore Einstein's own primary-source record of his thinking *at the moment* he was adopting the four-dimensional formalism. The McGucken FQXi compendium [MGFQXiCompendium] reproduces verbatim the three load-bearing passages from the 1912 manuscript in which Einstein explicitly writes $x_4 = ict$ and attributes the substitution to Minkowski. The first passage:

> *"If we compare this with the considerations leading to the general Lorentz transformation, then we see that the transformation equations holding between $x, y, z, u = ict$ and $x', y', z', u' = ict'$ of two justified space-time reference systems satisfy the same conditions and are constructed in the same way as in the just considered three-dimensional case. The only difference is that we now have four coordinates instead of three. We can formulate this in the following way: All of the 'justified' time-space reference systems to which the four-dimensional manifold of events is referred are orthogonal coordinate systems with four axes that can be transformed into each other by mere rotation. **One has to keep in mind that the fourth coordinate $u$ is always purely imaginary.**"* [Einstein1912Manuscript, with bold emphasis added by McGucken in the 2008 FQXi essay [MGFQXiCompendium]]

The second:

> *"If one introduces the variable $u = ict$ or $u' = ict'$ in place of the time variables $t$, where $i$ denotes the imaginary unit, one obtains, instead of (15a), the form $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + u^2 = x'^2 + y'^2 + z'^2 + u'^2$."* [Einstein1912Manuscript]

The third:

> *"As is well known, this choice of time variables derives from Minkowski. Its great significance consists in the fact that by means of it, equation (15a), which governs the substitution that we are seeking, is brought into a form into which the spatial coordinates and the temporal coordinate enter in the same manner."* [Einstein1912Manuscript]

The 1912 manuscript is therefore Einstein himself, in his own hand, in the year of his turn toward the four-dimensional formalism, explicitly writing the fourth coordinate $u = ict$, explicitly attributing the substitution to Minkowski, and explicitly stating that *"one has to keep in mind that the fourth coordinate $u$ is always purely imaginary."* The four-fold orthogonal-rotation structure that Minkowski 1908 had elevated to a physical-ontological reading and that Einstein 1920 would later exalt as the load-bearing formulation of general relativity is here, in 1912, recorded as Einstein's own working position. What is absent — and what the present paper identifies as the structural blind spot common to Poincaré 1905/1906, Minkowski 1908, and Einstein 1912/1920 — is any recognition that the imaginary fourth coordinate $u = ict$ might be the *integrated coordinate shadow* of an active physical-geometric process $dx_4/dt = ic$. Einstein wrote the integrated form; he did not see its dynamical source.

**The Misner–Thorne–Wheeler 1973 abandonment of $x_4 = ict$ (the integrated coordinate shadow of $dx_4/dt = ic$): the canonical pedagogical moment of the imaginary fourth coordinate's exile from general relativity.** Beyond the documented historical arc Poincaré 1905/1906 → Minkowski 1908 → Einstein 1908--1924 examined above, there is one further primary-source moment in the historical record that is structurally decisive for diagnosing why the McGucken Principle was not recovered in the twentieth century. The moment is the publication of Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler's *Gravitation* by W.\ H.\ Freeman and Company, San Francisco, in 1973 [MTW1973]. The 1279-page treatise — co-authored by Charles W.\ Misner (University of Maryland), Kip S.\ Thorne (California Institute of Technology), and John Archibald Wheeler (Princeton University) — is the canonical graduate-level general-relativity textbook of the late twentieth century, having trained essentially the entire community of working relativists from 1973 forward. The textbook's Chapter 2, "Foundations of Special Relativity," contains the precise passage in which $x_4 = ict$ is formally exiled from the canonical pedagogy of general relativity:

> *"In Lorentz-Minkowski geometry, when the interval between two events is zero, one event may be on Earth and the other on a supernova in the galaxy M31, but their separation must be a null ray (piece of a light cone). The backward-pointing light cone at a given event contains all the events by which that event can be influenced. The forward-pointing light cone contains all events that it can influence. The multitude of double light cones taking off from all the events of spacetime forms an interlocking causal structure. This structure makes the machinery of the physical world function as it does (further comments on this structure in Wheeler and Feynman 1945 and 1949 and in Zeeman 1964). If in a region where spacetime is flat, one can hide this structure from view by writing*
>
> *$(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x^1)^2 + (\Delta x^2)^2 + (\Delta x^3)^2 + (\Delta x^4)^2,$*
>
> *with $x^4 = ict$, no one has discovered a way to make an imaginary coordinate work in the general curved spacetime manifold. If '$x^4 = ict$' cannot be used there, it will not be used here. In this chapter and hereafter, as throughout the literature of general relativity, a real time coordinate is used, $x^0 = t = ct_{\mathrm{conv}}$ (superscript 0 rather than 4 to avoid any possibility of confusion with the imaginary time coordinate)."* [MTW1973, Chapter 2, §2.3]

The passage is the canonical 1973 statement of the abandonment of $x^4 = ict$ in graduate-level general-relativity pedagogy. Four structural observations follow from a close reading of the passage.

*First, the abandonment is pedagogical and conventional, not physical or mathematical.* MTW explicitly state that the $x^4 = ict$ formulation *works* in flat spacetime — they write the Minkowski interval $(\Delta s)^2 = (\Delta x^1)^2 + (\Delta x^2)^2 + (\Delta x^3)^2 + (\Delta x^4)^2$ in the imaginary-time form and immediately observe that this representation correctly captures the Lorentz-invariant interval. They acknowledge that the imaginary-time form *displays* the perpendicularity structure of the four-fold orthogonal Euclidean form that Einstein 1920 had identified as the load-bearing content of Minkowski's contribution [Einstein1920Relativity]. The grounds for abandonment given in the passage are not that the imaginary-time form is incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent. The grounds are *uniformity with the curved-spacetime case*: "no one has discovered a way to make an imaginary coordinate work in the general curved spacetime manifold."

*Second, the inference is a pedagogical preference for cross-case notational uniformity.* The implicit syllogism of the passage is: (i) the $ict$ formulation does not generalize to curved spacetime; (ii) general relativity is fundamentally about curved spacetime; therefore (iii) the $ict$ formulation will not be used in flat spacetime either. The third step does not follow from the first two by any mathematical or physical necessity. The third step is a *pedagogical decision* — favoring a uniform notation across flat and curved cases over the perpendicularity-content visibility of the flat-case imaginary-time formulation. The decision is one of textbook design, not of physics.

*Third, the cost of the abandonment is precisely what the present paper has been diagnosing.* By replacing $x^4 = ict$ with the real-coordinate $x^0 = ct$ uniformly across flat and curved cases, MTW 1973 concealed the perpendicularity content of the imaginary unit inside the metric tensor $\eta_{\mu\nu} = \mathrm{diag}(-1, +1, +1, +1)$. The Minkowski interval becomes $(\Delta s)^2 = -(\Delta x^0)^2 + (\Delta x^1)^2 + (\Delta x^2)^2 + (\Delta x^3)^2$, with the negative sign in front of $(\Delta x^0)^2$ now doing the load-bearing work that the imaginary unit $i$ in $x^4 = ict$ had done in the Poincaré 1905/1906 → Minkowski 1908 → Einstein 1912/1920 lineage. The substitution is mathematically equivalent at the level of the invariant interval, but it is *informationally lossy* at the level of geometric content: the negative sign in $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ conceals the fact that the fourth coordinate is physically perpendicular to the three spatial coordinates in the same Euclidean sense that the three spatial coordinates are mutually perpendicular. The four-fold orthogonal-rotation content that Einstein 1912 had explicitly stated ("orthogonal coordinate systems with four axes that can be transformed into each other by mere rotation") [Einstein1912Manuscript] is preserved formally in the $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ formulation but concealed visually and pedagogically.

The Huang–Zee–Wolfram–Feynman cluster examined in the previous subsections is a direct downstream consequence. By 1973 the $ict$ formulation had been removed from the canonical graduate-level pedagogy; by the late twentieth century essentially the entire community of working physicists had been trained in the real-coordinate $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ convention; the perpendicularity-factor content that had been visible to Einstein 1920 was no longer visible to the post-MTW community; the Wick rotation $t \to -i\tau$ that arises naturally as a coordinate identity on the $ict$-formulation manifold became a "calculational trick" with no apparent geometric content on the $\eta_{\mu\nu}$-formulation manifold; and the persistent admission that there is "something profound here that we have not quite understood" [Zee2003] is the residual diagnostic of the missing content.

*Fourth, and structurally decisive, the MTW 1973 abandonment is internally diagnostic of the McGucken lineage itself.* The 1973 *Gravitation* textbook is co-authored by John Archibald Wheeler, the present author's undergraduate advisor at Princeton 1989--1991 [Wheeler1990Recommendation]. Wheeler is therefore in the lineage that simultaneously codified the 1973 abandonment of $x^4 = ict$ in canonical pedagogy and, sixteen years later in 1989, directed the present author in Jadwin Hall at Princeton that "today's world lacks the noble... and it's your generation's duty to bring it back" [Wheeler1989Jadwin]. The structural irony is direct: Wheeler co-signed the textbook that exiled the imaginary fourth coordinate from canonical general relativity in 1973; Wheeler then directed the present author in 1989 to recover what the late-twentieth-century physics community had lost; the present author, taking Einstein's 1912 equation $x_4 = ict$ — written in Einstein's own hand and explicitly attributed to Minkowski [Einstein1912Manuscript] — and differentiating it with respect to $t$, recovered the dynamical content $dx_4/dt = ic$ that Einstein and Minkowski did not see and that Wheeler's 1973 textbook exiled. The 2026 McGucken corpus is the recovery; the McGucken Principle is the differentiation that the 1973 abandonment had made structurally invisible to the post-MTW pedagogy.

*The relevant note for completeness.* MTW's stated reason for the abandonment — that "no one has discovered a way to make an imaginary coordinate work in the general curved spacetime manifold" — is also addressed by the McGucken framework. The McGucken Geometry paper [MGGeometry] and the McGucken General Theory paper [MGGeneralRelativity] establish that the $dx_4/dt = ic$ structure extends naturally to curved spacetime via the McGucken–Kaluza–Klein extension, with the integrated coordinate shadow $x_4 = ict$ retained as the local content of the active-expansion principle at every event, and with general-covariant tensor structure preserved throughout. The MTW 1973 assertion that "no one has discovered" such a generalization was correct as of 1973; the present 2026 corpus contains the generalization. The 1973 abandonment was therefore a pedagogical decision made at a moment when the curved-spacetime extension of $x^4 = ict$ was not yet available; the 2026 corpus removes the structural reason for the abandonment by supplying the generalization. The exile of $x^4 = ict$ from canonical pedagogy is now structurally reversible, and the perpendicularity-content visibility of the imaginary fourth coordinate is now recoverable in both flat and curved cases under the McGucken Principle.

The MTW 1973 passage is therefore the canonical pedagogical-historical moment of the abandonment of the perpendicularity-content visibility that the McGucken Principle now restores at primary-source rigor. The reader is invited to compare three statements of the same underlying content: Einstein 1912 ("orthogonal coordinate systems with four axes that can be transformed into each other by mere rotation... one has to keep in mind that the fourth coordinate $u$ is always purely imaginary") [Einstein1912Manuscript]; Einstein 1920 ("the time co-ordinate plays exactly the same role as the three space co-ordinates") [Einstein1920Relativity]; MTW 1973 ("if '$x^4 = ict$' cannot be used there, it will not be used here") [MTW1973]. The McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ is the recovery of that content at the level of the dynamical source, with $x_4 = ict$ retained as its integrated coordinate shadow.

**The deeper structural distinction: MTW's symmetric-curvability framework versus the McGucken framework's $dx_4/dt = ic$-invariance with $x_1 x_2 x_3$-stationarity.** The MTW 1973 abandonment of $x^4 = ict$ in favor of $x^0 = ct$ is not merely a notational substitution. It encodes a substantive physical-geometric commitment that distinguishes the entire MTW/Wheeler/Misner/Thorne program from the McGucken framework at the level of how the four coordinates respond to the presence of matter.

*MTW's position: all four dimensions equally curvable by mass.* In the MTW 1973 framework, building on Einstein 1916 [Einstein1916GR], the four-dimensional spacetime manifold is described by a single metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ with sixteen components (ten independent under symmetry), every one of which is responsive to the matter distribution through Einstein's field equations

$$G_{\mu\nu} \;=\; \frac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu\nu}, \label{eq:einstein-field-eq}$$

where the Einstein tensor $G_{\mu\nu} = R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac{1}{2} R g_{\mu\nu}$ couples curvature to the stress-energy tensor $T_{\mu\nu}$ on the right-hand side. The four indices $\mu, \nu \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ are formally symmetric; the metric components $g_{00}, g_{0i}, g_{ij}$ for $i, j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ are all dynamical variables, all subject to bending and curving in response to matter, all on an equal footing in the field equations. This is the position MTW's adoption of the real-coordinate convention $x^0 = ct$ encodes structurally: by removing the imaginary unit $i$ that had distinguished $x^4 = ict$ from $(x^1, x^2, x^3)$ in the Einstein 1912/1920 formulation, MTW expresses formally that the time coordinate is one further coordinate alongside the three spatial coordinates, with no structural asymmetry between them. The bending and curving of the manifold by matter affects all four coordinates symmetrically; there is no preferred coordinate that remains invariant under matter aggregation.

*The McGucken framework's position: $dx_4/dt = ic$ is strictly invariant; $x_1 x_2 x_3$ are stationary-but-locally-curvable-by-mass.* The McGucken framework establishes, by the McGucken-Invariance Lemma [MGGeneralRelativity, Theorem 2], that the rate $dx_4/dt$ is *strictly invariant under gravity, acceleration, and every other physical condition* — never anywhere in the universe does $x_4$ advance at a rate other than $ic$. The fourth axis is *not* a coordinate that bends and curves in response to matter; it is the foundational invariant whose unyielding expansion at $+ic$ is the source of every other physical invariant. The three spatial dimensions $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are the curvable sector: they are *stationary in the absence of mass* (no global expansion) but they are *locally curvable by aggregated mass* through Scenario-A Schwarzschild stretching [McGuckenCosmology2026, §X.3b.1], where the radial metric coefficient $h_{rr} = (1 - r_s/r)^{-1} > 1$ records the local stretching of $x_1 x_2 x_3$ around a mass $M$ with Schwarzschild radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$. The physical mechanism of gravitational time dilation in the McGucken framework — established as a theorem of $dx_4/dt = ic$ by the Gravitational Time Dilation Theorem [McGuckenCosmology2026, §X.3b.3] — is that *the wristwatch ticks slower not because $dx_4/dt$ has changed (it has not; $dx_4/dt = ic$ is strictly invariant) but because the photon clock has more stretched $x_1 x_2 x_3$ to traverse while $x_4$ maintains its invariant $+ic$ expansion*. The principle stays invariant; the wristwatch responds to the stretched $x_1 x_2 x_3$.

The two positions are not notational variants of one underlying geometry. They are *physically distinct claims about how the four-dimensional manifold responds to matter*. MTW asserts symmetric-curvability across all four coordinates; the McGucken framework asserts $x_4$-invariance with $x_1 x_2 x_3$-curvability. The two claims make different physical predictions in the regimes where they bear on observable quantities, and the empirical record adjudicates between them — as the McGucken Cosmology paper [McGuckenCosmology2026] demonstrates with first-place finishes across twelve independent observational tests including the Hubble tension, the SPARC Radial Acceleration Relation, the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation slope of exactly 4, the Bullet Cluster dark-mass offset, the DESI 2024–2025 dark-energy $w(z)$ evolution, the ACT DR6 cosmological parameters, the CMB preferred-frame existence, the horizon and flatness problems without inflation, and the cosmological-scale-factor evolution under the hypothesis $C$ hybrid configuration most consistent with the DESI 2024 results.

*The formal proof of the McGucken asymmetry: the Disjunctive Forcing Theorem.* The asymmetry between $x_4$ and $x_1 x_2 x_3$ in the McGucken framework is not a postulate of the theory; it is *formally proved* by the Disjunctive Forcing Theorem of [McGuckenCosmology2026, §X.7.5]. The theorem establishes by case-exhaustion that any candidate dynamical principle $\Pi$ governing the rate and direction of advance of the fourth coordinate $x_4$ either is the McGucken Principle $dx_4/dt = ic$ with sphere-surface $x_4$-locality, or fails by orders of magnitude on at least one of five empirically settled strands of physics: (i) Tsirelson saturation of the CHSH Bell inequality at $|\mathrm{CHSH}| = 2\sqrt{2}$ across loophole-free Bell tests; (ii) rotational invariance of entanglement correlations under SO(3) with no preferred spatial direction; (iii) absence of any entanglement-distance limit (the Micius satellite Bell test at 1200 km finds $|\mathrm{CHSH}| = 2.37 \pm 0.09$, forcing the coherence length $L_{\mathrm{coh}} > 10^8$ m, larger than the Earth-Moon distance); (iv) Lorentz invariance of $c$ at parts in $10^{-20}$ across photon energies and over gigaparsec distances (the GRB 090510 timing bound of Vasileiou et al.\ 2013); and (v) sharp Huygens propagation: every point on a wavefront is the apex of a new spherical wavelet whose envelope forms the future wavefront, so that disturbances propagate along the light cone with no tail in its interior. *Audit-rigor note on strand (v):* the wave equation $\Box \psi = 0$ in $3+1$ dimensions has a retarded Green's function $G_{\mathrm{ret}}(x, t; x', t') = \delta(t - t' - |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'|/c)/(4\pi |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}'|)$ supported on the light cone (Hadamard 1923 [Hadamard1923]); the failure of strong Huygens in even spatial dimensions or in the presence of mass terms produces a Green's function with support in the full interior of the past light cone, contradicting the empirical sharpness of light propagation rather than negating Green's-function existence per se. The Mode E exclusion is therefore *empirical sharpness* of light propagation, not the formal absence of a Green's function.

The case-exhaustion is exhaustive across three orthogonal structural axes: the rate of $x_4$-advance (direction-independent of magnitude $c$ vs.\ direction-dependent); the surface assignment of the $x_4$-coordinate on the McGucken Sphere (constant zero vs.\ stochastic, systematic-gradient, finite-thickness, or undefined); and the orientation $\pm ic$ (fixed by the thermodynamic arrow of time at $+ic$). - Birkhoff's ergodic theorem on time-averages equaling space-averages on ergodic systems [Birkhoff1931].
- Lindeberg-Lévy Central Limit Theorem on the convergence of i.i.d.\ sums to Gaussians [Lindeberg].
- Klein's Erlangen program on the classification of geometries by their symmetry groups [Klein1872].

- Ostrogradsky's theorem on higher-derivative theories [Ostrogradsky].
- KAM theorem (Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser) on the persistence of invariant tori in nearly-integrable Hamiltonian systems [Kolmogorov, Arnold, Moser].
- Noether's theorem on the correspondence between continuous symmetries and conservation laws [Noether].
